key_insight: Combine smaller generative draft trees with retrieval-augmented candidate expansion (a hybrid tree) so you 'draft less' but 'retrieve more', preserving high acceptance rates while cutting VRAM bandwidth and compute overhead for speculative decoding.
problem_solved: Large, expansive draft trees maximize acceptance but cause severe VRAM bandwidth and computational bottlenecks; dynamic pruning reduces latency but can throw away valid candidates and limit acceptance rate.
method: Construct a hybrid draft tree that keeps generative branching shallow (draft less) and fills high-quality continuation branches by retrieving candidates from a cache/datastore (retrieve more).
Apply selective pruning that prioritizes retrieval-backed branches to remove low-value generative branches without discarding likely valid candidates.
Verify retrieved + drafted candidates with the target model under the speculative decoding accept/reject check, maintaining high acceptance while reducing memory and compute traffic.
impact: Delivers higher end-to-end LLM inference throughput with much lower VRAM bandwidth and compute cost, making speculative decoding more practical on constrained hardware and improving latency in production systems.
visual_elements: Hybrid-tree diagram: small generative root with many retrieved branch leaves (labels: 'draft' vs 'retrieved').
Pipeline flowchart: draft → retrieve → prune → verify, highlighting reduced VRAM/computation at the prune step.
Bar chart: comparison of throughput, VRAM bandwidth, and acceptance rate for (large-draft tree) vs (hybrid tree).
Line plot or heatmap: acceptance rate vs tree size/pruning aggressiveness showing hybrid approach near the upper bound with lower resource use.
paper_title: Draft Less, Retrieve More: Hybrid Tree Construction for Speculative Decoding
paper_authors: Yuhao Shen, Tianyu Liu, Xinyi Hu, Quan Kong, Baolin Zhang
